claim: C. elegans males exhibit an altered, male-specific expression pattern of daf-7 in the ASJ sensory neuron pair with the onset of reproductive maturity.
source: Here, we show that C. elegans males exhibit an altered, male-specific expression pattern of daf-7 in the ASJ sensory neuron pair with the onset of reproductive maturity, which functions to promote male-specific mate-searching behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing pdaf-7::gfp expression and FISH results in males versus hermaphrodites, and developmental time course data.

claim: Male-specific daf-7 expression in ASJ functions to promote male-specific mate-searching behavior.
source: Here, we show that C. elegans males exhibit an altered, male-specific expression pattern of daf-7 in the ASJ sensory neuron pair with the onset of reproductive maturity, which functions to promote male-specific mate-searching behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral assays showing daf-7 mutants and ASJ-ablated males have defects in mate-searching behavior.

claim: Regulation of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair reveals a hierarchy of regulation among multiple inputs: sex, age, nutritional status, and microbial environment.
source: Molecular genetic analysis of the switch-like regulation of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair reveals a hierarchy of regulation among multiple inputs—sex, age, nutritional status, and microbial environment—which function in the modulation of behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects of these inputs on daf-7 expression.

claim: Regulation of gene expression in sensory neurons can function in the integration of a wide array of sensory information and facilitate decision-making behaviors in C. elegans.
source: Our results suggest that regulation of gene expression in sensory neurons can function in the integration of a wide array of sensory information and facilitate decision-making behaviors in C. elegans.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental results showing multiple inputs regulating daf-7 in ASJ neurons.

claim: Adult males exhibit daf-7 expression in both the ASI and the ASJ neuron pairs in the absence of P. aeruginosa.
source: In the current study, we observed that adult males exhibit daf-7 expression in both the ASI and the ASJ neuron pairs in the absence of P. aeruginosa (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by pdaf-7::gfp reporter data and FISH data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The expression pattern difference in adult C. elegans can be observed through the use of a pdaf-7::gfp transcriptional reporter.
source: This expression pattern difference in adult C. elegans, can be observed both through the use of a pdaf-7::gfp transcriptional reporter (Figure 1A and B) as well as by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) that directly probes for endogenous daf-7 mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using the pdaf-7::gfp reporter shown in figures.

claim: The expression pattern difference in adult C. elegans can be observed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) that directly probes for endogenous daf-7 mRNA.
source: This expression pattern difference in adult C. elegans, can be observed both through the use of a pdaf-7::gfp transcriptional reporter (Figure 1A and B) as well as by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) that directly probes for endogenous daf-7 mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by FISH experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: In populations of early larval animals carrying the pdaf-7::gfp transcriptional reporter, males and hermaphrodites are indistinguishable, with fluorescence observed only in the ASI neurons.
source: We observed that in populations of early larval animals carrying the pdaf-7::gfp transcriptional reporter, males and hermaphrodites were indistinguishable, with fluorescence observed only in the ASI neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: daf-7 expression remains off in the ASJ of males through the end of the last (L4) larval stage, but is switched on during young adulthood as the animals reach reproductive maturity.
source: We found that daf-7 expression remains off in the ASJ of males through the end of the last (L4) larval stage, but is switched on during young adulthood as the animals reach reproductive maturity (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a significant drop in the expression of daf-7 in the ASI neurons from L4 to young adulthood in males.
source: In addition, we examined expression of daf-7 in the ASI neuron pair at several matched timepoints during development and observed a significant drop in the expression of daf-7 in the ASI neurons from L4 to young adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and F, 52 hr and 64.5 hr timepoints).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and F.

claim: At subsequent timepoints during adulthood, expression levels in the ASI neurons remained constant as expression in the ASJ neurons increased.
source: At subsequent timepoints during adulthood, however, expression levels in the ASI neurons remained constant as expression in the ASJ neurons increased (Figure 1—figure supplements 1E,3F 64.5 hr and 71.5 hr timepoints).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and F.

claim: In tra-1(e1099) mutant XX males, daf-7 expression can be seen in both the ASI and ASJ neurons.
source: In these mutant XX males, daf-7 expression could be seen in both the ASI and ASJ neurons, suggesting that daf-7 is regulated by the genetic sex determination pathway either directly or indirectly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: daf-7 is regulated by the genetic sex determination pathway either directly or indirectly.
source: In these mutant XX males, daf-7 expression could be seen in both the ASI and ASJ neurons, suggesting that daf-7 is regulated by the genetic sex determination pathway either directly or indirectly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on inference from tra-1 mutant data showing male-like daf-7 expression in XX animals.

claim: Expression of FEM-3 cDNA under the control of the pan-neural promoter, rab-3, leads to up-regulation of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons of adult hermaphrodites.
source: We expressed the FEM-3 cDNA under the control of the pan-neural promoter, rab-3, and found that daf-7 expression was up-regulated in the ASJ neurons of adult hermaphrodites, suggesting that a genetically 'male' nervous system is sufficient for daf-7 expression in ASJ (Figure 2A, C and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, C and E.

claim: A genetically 'male' nervous system is sufficient for daf-7 expression in ASJ.
source: We expressed the FEM-3 cDNA under the control of the pan-neural promoter, rab-3, and found that daf-7 expression was up-regulated in the ASJ neurons of adult hermaphrodites, suggesting that a genetically 'male' nervous system is sufficient for daf-7 expression in ASJ (Figure 2A, C and E).
evidence: Based on inference from masculinization experiments showing daf-7 expression in genetically masculinized hermaphrodites.

claim: The overall expression of daf-7 in the ASJ of masculinized hermaphrodites is notably lower than what is observed in wild-type males.
source: Although we observed an increase in daf-7 expression in these genetically masculinized animals, the overall expression of daf-7 in the ASJ of masculinized hermaphrodites was still notably lower than what we observe in wild-type males (e.g. Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of quantitative data between masculinized hermaphrodites and wild-type males.

claim: Males of ceh-30(n4289), mab-3(e1240), and pkd-2(sy606);lov-1(sy582) mutant strains retain wild-type expression levels of daf-7 in ASJ.
source: Males of all mutant strains retained wild-type expression levels of daf-7 in ASJ, suggesting that the male-specific neural circuitry is not required for daf-7 expression and is unlikely to underlie the lower daf-7 expression we see in genetically masculinized hermaphrodites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The male-specific neural circuitry is not required for daf-7 expression.
source: Males of all mutant strains retained wild-type expression levels of daf-7 in ASJ, suggesting that the male-specific neural circuitry is not required for daf-7 expression and is unlikely to underlie the lower daf-7 expression we see in genetically masculinized hermaphrodites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on inference from mutant data showing normal daf-7 expression despite loss of male-specific neurons.

claim: The male-specific neural circuitry is unlikely to underlie the lower daf-7 expression seen in genetically masculinized hermaphrodites.
source: Males of all mutant strains retained wild-type expression levels of daf-7 in ASJ, suggesting that the male-specific neural circuitry is not required for daf-7 expression and is unlikely to underlie the lower daf-7 expression we see in genetically masculinized hermaphrodites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on inference from mutant data showing normal daf-7 expression despite loss of male-specific neurons.

claim: Overexpression of TRA-2IC under the control of the rab-3 promoter leads to complete loss of daf-7 expression in the ASJ of otherwise male animals.
source: Overexpression of TRA-2IC under the control of the rab-3 promoter led to complete loss of daf-7 expression in the ASJ of otherwise male animals (Figure 2B, D and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, D and F.

claim: A genetically male nervous system is both necessary and sufficient for the sex-specific expression pattern of daf-7.
source: These results suggest that a genetically male nervous system is both necessary and sufficient for the sex-specific expression pattern of daf-7.
evidence: Based on inference from masculinization and feminization experiments.

claim: Masculinization of only the ASJ neuron pair using the trx-1 ASJ-specific promoter results in no daf-7 expression in adult hermaphrodites.
source: Using the trx-1 ASJ-specific promoter, we masculinized the ASJ neuron pair alone and saw no daf-7 expression in the resulting adult hermaphrodites (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No daf-7 expression can be observed when only the ciliated neurons are masculinized.
source: Similarly, no daf-7 expression could be observed when only the ciliated neurons (of which ASJ is a member) were masculinized (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: An additional neuron (or neurons) or other tissues require a male cell identity for daf-7 to be expressed in the ASJ neurons.
source: These data suggest the requirement that an additional neuron (or neurons) or other tissues have a male cell identity for daf-7 to be expressed in the ASJ neurons, although differences in the strength of the heterologous promoters used in the masculinization constructs may also account for these observations.
evidence: Based on inference from cell-specific masculinization experiments showing insufficient daf-7 expression.

claim: Both ciliated neuron-specific and ASJ-specific feminization in males lead to down-regulation of daf-7 expression.
source: In contrast, both ciliated neuron-specific and ASJ-specific feminization in males led to down-regulation of daf-7 expression, confirming that a male cell identity in ASJ is necessary, though not sufficient, for proper daf-7 expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A male cell identity in ASJ is necessary, though not sufficient, for proper daf-7 expression.
source: In contrast, both ciliated neuron-specific and ASJ-specific feminization in males led to down-regulation of daf-7 expression, confirming that a male cell identity in ASJ is necessary, though not sufficient, for proper daf-7 expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: Based on inference from feminization experiments showing loss of daf-7 expression.

claim: Mutants in both the DAF-7/TGF-β ligand and its Type I receptor, DAF-1, show defects in the mate-searching assay.
source: We observed that mutants in both the DAF-7/TGF-β ligand and its Type I receptor, DAF-1, showed defects in the mate-searching assay (Figure 3A and B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3A and B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The behavioral defect in the daf-7 mutant can be fully suppressed by mutation of the downstream antagonistic co-SMAD, DAF-3.
source: This behavioral defect in the daf-7 mutant can be fully suppressed by mutation of the downstream antagonistic co-SMAD, DAF-3, suggesting that DAF-7 functions through its canonical TGF-β signaling pathway to regulate mate-searching behavior (Figure 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DAF-7 functions through its canonical TGF-β signaling pathway to regulate mate-searching behavior.
source: This behavioral defect in the daf-7 mutant can be fully suppressed by mutation of the downstream antagonistic co-SMAD, DAF-3, suggesting that DAF-7 functions through its canonical TGF-β signaling pathway to regulate mate-searching behavior (Figure 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on inference from genetic suppression data showing daf-3 mutation rescues daf-7 mutant phenotype.

claim: ASJ-ablated animals are defective in mate-searching behavior.
source: We observed that the ASJ-ablated animals were defective in mate-searching behavior, establishing a role for the ASJ neuron pair in promoting this behavior (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ASJ neuron pair has a role in promoting mate-searching behavior.
source: We observed that the ASJ-ablated animals were defective in mate-searching behavior, establishing a role for the ASJ neuron pair in promoting this behavior (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on inference from ASJ ablation experiments showing defects in mate-searching.

claim: The defects in daf-7 mutant and ASJ-ablated male behavior are not accounted for by global defects in locomotion.
source: Importantly, the defects that we see in daf-7 mutant and ASJ-ablated male behavior are not accounted for by global defects in locomotion. When mutant animals are tested on leaving assay plates on which the bacterial food has been fully spread, these males reach the scoring distance at equivalent rates to WT controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Barrios et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by locomotion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and cited reference.

claim: The reduced leaving behavior observed in daf-7 mutant and ASJ-ablated animals is specific to the decision to leave the food source in search of a mate.
source: This suggests that the reduced leaving behavior we observe in these animals isspecific to the decision to leave the food source in search of a mate.
evidence: Based on inference from locomotion control experiments showing normal movement on full lawns.

claim: Transgenic rescue of daf-7 from the endogenous promoter as well as from ASI- and ASJ-specific promoters is sufficient to restore mate-searching behavior in the daf-7(ok3125) mutant background.
source: As expected, we saw that transgenic rescue from the endogenous promoter as well as from ASI- and ASJ-specific promoters were sufficient to restore mate-searching behavior in the daf-7(ok3125) mutant background (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The dynamic expression of daf-7 in the ASJ neurons of adult males regulates mate-searching behavior.
source: Taken together, these data imply that the dynamic expression of daf-7 in the ASJ neurons of adult males regulates mate-searching behavior.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including expression patterns, mutant phenotypes, and rescue experiments.

claim: Males subjected to starvation beginning early in the L4 larval stage fail to express daf-7 in the ASJ neurons as adults.
source: We found that males subjected to starvation beginning early in the L4 larval stage failed to express daf-7 in the ASJ neurons as adults (Figure 4A, conditions i and ii, and Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The lack of daf-7 in the ASJ neuron pair during starvation is apparent both by GFP visualization as well as by FISH, with daf-7 mRNA entirely absent from the ASJ neurons.
source: This lack of daf-7 in the ASJ neuron pair was apparent both by GFP visualization as well as by FISH, with daf-7 mRNA entirely absent from the ASJ neurons (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: daf-7 mRNA is still apparent in the ASI, OLQ, and ADE neurons of starved animals.
source: We noticed that daf-7 mRNA was still apparent in the ASI, OLQ, and ADE neurons of these starved animals, suggesting that the loss of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons is specific and not representative of a global down-regulation of transcription in these animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons during starvation is specific and not representative of a global down-regulation of transcription.
source: We noticed that daf-7 mRNA was still apparent in the ASI, OLQ, and ADE neurons of these starved animals, suggesting that the loss of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons is specific and not representative of a global down-regulation of transcription in these animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on inference from FISH data showing daf-7 expression in other neurons during starvation.

claim: In animals that experienced starvation during the L4-to-adulthood period before being returned to an E. coli food source as adults, daf-7 expression can be detected both by the GFP reporter as well as by FISH.
source: We first looked at daf-7 expression in animals that had experienced starvation during the L4-to-adulthood period before being returned to an E. coli food source as adults. In these animals, daf-7 expression could be detected both by the GFP reporter as well as by FISH (Figure 4A, condition iii, and 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: When males are allowed to develop into adulthood unperturbed and then subjected to a period of food deprivation, a complete loss of daf-7 mRNA in the ASJ neurons is observed.
source: When males were allowed to develop into adulthood unperturbed and then subjected to a period of food deprivation, we observed a complete loss of daf-7 mRNA in the ASJ neurons (Figure 4A, condition iv).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons is subject to dynamic regulation by periods of starvation and re-feeding.
source: Together this data demonstrates that daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons is subject to dynamic regulation by periods of starvation and re-feeding.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple starvation and re-feeding experiments.

claim: daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair is not significantly increased compared to starved controls until 9 hr after the re-introduction of an E. coli food source.
source: We observed that daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair is not significantly increased compared to starved controls until 9 hr after the re-introduction of an E. coli food source (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by time course data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The extended period of time required to restore daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair suggests that internal nutritional state, not the chemosensation of bacterial food, exerts control over daf-7 transcription in the ASJ neuron pair.
source: The extended period of time required to restore daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair suggests that internal nutritional state, not the chemosensation of bacterial food, exerts control over daf-7 transcription in the ASJ neuron pair.
evidence: Based on inference from the slow kinetics of daf-7 re-expression after re-feeding.

claim: The onset of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons of males following the re-introduction of food is consistent with the previously noted kinetics of resumption of mate-searching behavior after males have been starved.
source: Moreover, we observed that the onset of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons of males following the re-introduction of food are consistent with the previously noted kinetics of resumption of mate-searching behavior after males have been starved (Figure 4C; Lipton et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by comparison with behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and cited reference.

claim: When transferred to P. aeruginosa, males carrying the pdaf-7::gfp transcriptional reporter exhibit an increase in daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons compared to E. coli-fed controls.
source: We observe that, when transferred to P. aeruginosa, males carrying the pdaf-7::gfp transcriptional reporter exhibited an increase in daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons compared to E. coli-fed controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ASJ neuron pair of males retain the ability to respond to P. aeruginosa that is observed in hermaphrodites.
source: The additive nature of DAF-7 levels in males suggests that the ASJ neuron pair of males retain the ability to respond to P. aeruginosa that we observe in hermaphrodites.
evidence: Based on inference from the additive increase in daf-7 expression in males exposed to P. aeruginosa.

claim: A rapid up-regulation of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons of starved males returned to P. aeruginosa as a food source is observed.
source: Looking at animals carrying the pdaf-7::gfp reporter during post-starvation re-feeding, we observed a rapid up-regulation of daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons of starved males returned to P. aeruginosa as a food source (Figure 5A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The increase in daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair can be seen as early as 2 hr after first exposure to the pathogenic bacteria.
source: This increase in daf-7 expression in the ASJ neuron pair could be seen as early as 2 hr after first exposure to the pathogenic bacteria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by time course data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Starved males that are returned to the non-pathogenic E. coli show little to no daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons until much later time points.
source: In contrast, starved males that were returned to the non-pathogenic E. coli showed little to no daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons until much later time points (Figure 5A,B and 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B and 4B.

claim: The kinetics of the increase in fluorescence of the pdaf-7::gfp reporter in response to P. aeruginosa secondary metabolites lags behind the immediate response observed by FISH and is consistent with what was observed previously for hermaphrodite animals.
source: The kinetics of the increase in fluorescence of the pdaf-7::gfp reporter in response to P. aeruginosa secondary metabolites, which lags behind the immediate response observed by FISH is consistent with what we observed previously for hermaphrodite animals (Meisel et al., 2014), and notably faster than the slower increase in pdaf-7::gfp reporter fluorescence in response to repletion of the non-pathogenic E. coli bacterial food.
evidence: Supported by comparison with previously published data and current experimental observations.

claim: Starved males who are returned to a lawn of P. aeruginosa will readily leave the bacterial lawn at a rate similar to non-starved animals on the normal E. coli food source.
source: Indeed, whereas starved males will remain on the E. coli lawn for several hours, starved males who are instead returned to a lawn of P. aeruginosa will readily leave the bacterial lawn at a rate similar to non-starved animals on the normal E. coli food source (Figures 4C and 5C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figures 4C and 5C.

claim: Both fed and starved hermaphrodites will readily leave a lawn of P. aeruginosa.
source: This lawn-leaving behavior is not male-specific, as both fed and starved hermaphrodites will also readily leave a lawn of P. aeruginosa and starved hermaphrodites are also capable of responding to P. aeruginosa through an upregulation of daf-7 in the ASJ neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–1D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral and expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–1D.

claim: Starved hermaphrodites are capable of responding to P. aeruginosa through an upregulation of daf-7 in the ASJ neurons.
source: This lawn-leaving behavior is not male-specific, as both fed and starved hermaphrodites will also readily leave a lawn of P. aeruginosa and starved hermaphrodites are also capable of responding to P. aeruginosa through an upregulation of daf-7 in the ASJ neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–1D).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–1D.

claim: daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons is one way through which animals are able to interpret internal and external cues and prioritize their behaviors accordingly.
source: Our data suggest that daf-7 expression in the ASJ neurons is one way through which animals are both able to interpret internal and external cues and prioritize their behaviors accordingly.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experiments showing daf-7 regulation by different inputs and effects on behavior.

claim: Modulation of daf-7 expression provides an example of how a neuroendocrine signaling pathway may be coopted to guide behavioral decisions in entirely different contexts.
source: Our data suggest that modulation of daf-7 expression provides a striking example of how a neuroendocrine signaling pathway may be coopted to guide behavioral decisions in entirely different contexts.
evidence: Based on inference from the dual role of daf-7 in pathogen avoidance and mate-searching.

claim: The transcriptional regulation of daf-7 in the ASJ neurons functions as an ON/OFF switch, where each input holds the switch in one of two states.
source: The work presented here suggests that the transcriptional regulation of daf-7 in the ASJ neurons functions as an ON/OFF switch, where each input holds the switch—and thus, daf-7 expression—in one of two states.
evidence: Based on inference from the binary nature of daf-7 expression patterns observed under different conditions.

claim: The various regulatory inputs into the daf-7 transcriptional switch exert differential control, with environmental cues being prioritized over all others.
source: However, the various regulatory inputs into this switch exert differential control, with environmental cues being prioritized over all others.
evidence: Based on inference from the hierarchy of responses observed in starvation and pathogen exposure experiments.

claim: The differential control of the transcriptional switch allows for re-adjustments of behavioral priorities in the worm based on its current and past experience.
source: This differential control of the transcriptional switch, in turn allows for re-adjustments of behavioral priorities in the worm based on its current and past experience.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed behavioral changes in response to different environmental and internal state conditions.

claim: Expression of the chemoreceptor, ODR-10, in the sex-shared sensory AWA neurons has been shown to be dependent on both internal and external cues to regulate food-related decision making in male C. elegans.
source: Expression of the chemoreceptor, ODR-10, in the sex-shared sensory AWA neurons has also been shown to be dependent on both internal and external cues to regulate food-related decision making in male C. elegans (Ryan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2014.

claim: DAF-7/TGF-β has previously been found to be involved in the regulation of other satiety-regulated behaviors such as quiescence and foraging.
source: DAF-7/TGF-β has previously been found to be involved in the regulation of other satiety-regulated behaviors such as quiescence and foraging (Gallagher et al., 2013; Milward et al., 2011; You et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gallagher et al., 2013; Milward et al., 2011; You et al., 2008.

claim: daf-7 mutants show marked defects in the ability to respond to fasting through an increase in quiescence.
source: daf-7 mutants show marked defects in the ability to respond to fasting through an increase in quiescence, suggesting that DAF-7 may serve as a critical signal of food availability in the worm (You et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to You et al., 2008.

claim: DAF-7 may serve as a critical signal of food availability in the worm.
source: daf-7 mutants show marked defects in the ability to respond to fasting through an increase in quiescence, suggesting that DAF-7 may serve as a critical signal of food availability in the worm (You et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on inference from cited work showing daf-7 mutant defects in fasting response.

claim: DAF-7 signaling has been implicated in promoting food-leaving (or foraging) in the context of a rapidly depleting food source.
source: Similarly, DAF-7 signaling has also been implicated in promoting food-leaving (or foraging) in the context of a rapidly depleting food source, further underscoring the importance of this pathway for communicating nutritional availability (Milward et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milward et al., 2011.

claim: The daf-7 pathway may act as a more global food signal that is critical for allowing the animal to sense food and satiety and modulate its behaviors accordingly.
source: Taken together with our data, the important role of daf-7 in these different behavioral paradigms suggests that the daf-7 pathway may act as a more global food signal that is critical for allowing the animal to sense food and satiety and modulate its behaviors accordingly.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence about daf-7's role in various food-related behaviors.

claim: Integration of internal and external sensory information can occur at the level of the sensory neuron itself to regulate behavioral prioritization.
source: Finally, our results support a model where integration of internal and external sensory information can occur at the level of the sensory neuron itself to regulate behavioral prioritization.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's findings on daf-7 regulation in ASJ neurons.

claim: The data on the role of the ASJ sensory neurons in male mate-searching behavior are consistent with emerging evidence from studies in several species suggesting that the regulatory control of sensory neurons contributes to information processing and decision making behavior.
source: Our data on the role of the ASJ sensory neurons in male mate-searching behavior are consistent with emerging evidence from studies in several species to suggest that the regulatory control of sensory neurons contributes to information processing and decision making behavior (Dey et al., 2015; Lebreton et al., 2015; Peckol et al., 2001; Ryan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dey et al., 2015; Lebreton et al., 2015; Peckol et al., 2001; Ryan et al., 2014.

claim: The expression pattern of daf-7 was originally identified as being restricted to a single bilaterally symmetric pair of neurons in the head of the worm, the ASI chemosensory neurons.
source: The expression pattern of daf-7 was originally identified as being restricted to a single bilaterally symmetric pair of neurons in the head of the worm, the ASI chemosensory neurons, but it is also expressed in the ADE and OLQ neurons under normal laboratory growth conditions (Meisel et al., 2014; Ren et al., 1996; Schackwitz et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meisel et al., 2014; Ren et al., 1996; Schackwitz et al., 1996.

claim: daf-7 is also expressed in the ADE and OLQ neurons under normal laboratory growth conditions.
source: The expression pattern of daf-7 was originally identified as being restricted to a single bilaterally symmetric pair of neurons in the head of the worm, the ASI chemosensory neurons, but it is also expressed in the ADE and OLQ neurons under normal laboratory growth conditions (Meisel et al., 2014; Ren et al., 1996; Schackwitz et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meisel et al., 2014; Ren et al., 1996; Schackwitz et al., 1996.

claim: Within minutes of being exposed to P. aeruginosa, daf-7 expression is induced in the ASJ neurons in hermaphrodites, which in turn promotes behavioral avoidance of the pathogenic bacterial lawn.
source: Within minutes of being exposed to P. aeruginosa, daf-7 expression is induced in an additional pair of chemosensory neurons, the ASJ neurons, which in turn promotes behavioral avoidance of the pathogenic bacterial lawn (Meisel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meisel et al., 2014.

claim: C. elegans exist as one of two sexes: hermaphrodite or male.
source: C. elegans exist as one of two sexes: hermaphrodite or male.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about C. elegans biology.

claim: Hermaphrodites produce a limited amount of sperm during larval development making them capable of self-fertilization in addition to cross-fertilization.
source: Hermaphrodites produce a limited amount of sperm during larval development making them capable of self-fertilization in addition to cross-fertilization.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about C. elegans hermaphrodite reproduction.

claim: Males are only cross-fertile and must find mating partners for reproduction.
source: In contrast, males are only cross-fertile and must find mating partners for reproduction.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about C. elegans male reproduction.

claim: The male displays a large behavioral repertoire primarily aimed at facilitating mate finding and successful mating encounters.
source: As such, the male displays a large behavioral repertoire primarily aimed at facilitating mate finding and successful mating encounters.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about C. elegans male behavior.

claim: Male behaviors include complex mating rituals.
source: These behaviors include complex mating rituals (Liu and Sternberg, 1995), differential sensitivity to hermaphrodite pheromone (Srinivasan et al., 2008), and a mate-searching behavior in adult male animals that is driven by the prioritization of mating over feeding (Lipton et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu and Sternberg, 1995.

claim: Male behaviors include differential sensitivity to hermaphrodite pheromone.
source: These behaviors include complex mating rituals (Liu and Sternberg, 1995), differential sensitivity to hermaphrodite pheromone (Srinivasan et al., 2008), and a mate-searching behavior in adult male animals that is driven by the prioritization of mating over feeding (Lipton et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srinivasan et al., 2008.

claim: Male behaviors include a mate-searching behavior in adult male animals that is driven by the prioritization of mating over feeding.
source: These behaviors include complex mating rituals (Liu and Sternberg, 1995), differential sensitivity to hermaphrodite pheromone (Srinivasan et al., 2008), and a mate-searching behavior in adult male animals that is driven by the prioritization of mating over feeding (Lipton et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lipton et al., 2004.

claim: Mate-searching behavior of C. elegans is subject to regulation by multiple features of internal state—sex, age, and nutritional status—as well as by external sensory experiences such as the presence of food or hermaphrodites in the environment.
source: Mate-searching behavior of C. elegans has thus emerged as an interesting case study of decision making in a simple animal, which is subject to regulation by multiple features of internal state—sex, age, and nutritional status—as well as by external sensory experiences such as the presence of food or hermaphrodites in the environment (Barrios et al., 2008; Lipton et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrios et al., 2008; Lipton et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2014.

claim: The DAF-7/TGF-β signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in the regulation of diverse aspects of C. elegans physiology and behavior including the dauer developmental decision, reproductive egg laying, feeding and foraging, fat storage, satiety quiescence, longevity, aggregation, aerotaxis and avoidance of pathogenic bacteria.
source: Here, we focus on the DAF-7/TGF-β signaling pathway, which plays a pivotal role in the regulation of diverse aspects of C. elegans physiology and behavior including the dauer developmental decision, reproductive egg laying, feeding and foraging, fat storage, satiety quiescence, longevity, aggregation, aerotaxis and avoidance of pathogenic bacteria (Chang et al., 2006; Gallagher et al., 2013; Greer et al., 2008; Meisel et al., 2014; Milward et al., 2011; Ren et al., 1996; Shaw et al., 2007; White and Jorgensen, 2012; You et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang et al., 2006; Gallagher et al., 2013; Greer et al., 2008; Meisel et al., 2014; Milward et al., 2011; Ren et al., 1996; Shaw et al., 2007; White and Jorgensen, 2012; You et al., 2008.

claim: Mate-searching behavior has been demonstrated to be dependent on the feeding state of the animal—starved male animals will re-prioritize feeding over mate searching for a limited period of time until the animal has had sufficient opportunity to re-feed.
source: Mate-searching behavior has been demonstrated to be dependent on the feeding state of the animal—starved male animals will re-prioritize feeding over mate searching for a limited period of time until the animal has had sufficient opportunity to re-feed (Figure 4C; Lipton et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lipton et al., 2004 and data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TRA-1 activity functions to promote hermaphrodite cell fates and inhibit male development.
source: The C. elegans sex determination pathway terminates on the master regulator GLI-family transcription factor, TRA-1 (Zarkower and Hodgkin, 1992; Zarkower, 2006). TRA-1 activity functions to promote hermaphrodite cell fates and inhibit male development.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zarkower and Hodgkin, 1992; Zarkower, 2006.

claim: tra-1(e1099) mutants are karyotypically XX, but develop as fertile pseudomales due to the lack of active TRA-1.
source: We first looked at tra-1(e1099) mutants which are karyotypically XX, but develop as fertile pseudomales due to the lack of active TRA-1 (Hodgkin and Brenner, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hodgkin and Brenner, 1977.

claim: TRA-1 is negatively regulated by the FEM proteins—FEM-1, FEM-2, and FEM-3.
source: TRA-1 is negatively regulated by the FEM proteins—FEM-1, FEM-2, and FEM-3—and it has been demonstrated by many groups that overexpression of FEM-3 cDNA is sufficient to lead to 'masculinization' in otherwise hermaphrodite animals (Mehra et al., 1999; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Pereira et al., 2015; Sammut et al., 2015; White et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mehra et al., 1999; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Pereira et al., 2015; Sammut et al., 2015; White et al., 2007.

claim: Overexpression of FEM-3 cDNA is sufficient to lead to 'masculinization' in otherwise hermaphrodite animals.
source: TRA-1 is negatively regulated by the FEM proteins—FEM-1, FEM-2, and FEM-3—and it has been demonstrated by many groups that overexpression of FEM-3 cDNA is sufficient to lead to 'masculinization' in otherwise hermaphrodite animals (Mehra et al., 1999; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Pereira et al., 2015; Sammut et al., 2015; White et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mehra et al., 1999; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Pereira et al., 2015; Sammut et al., 2015; White et al., 2007.

claim: Genetic masculinization is effective in sexualizing neurons of the sex-shared nervous system, but fails to reliably retain the male-specific CEM neurons and produces hermaphrodites which also lack other male-specific neurons found in the tail.
source: While genetic masculinization is effective in sexualizing neurons of the sex-shared nervous system, this technique fails to reliably retain the male-specific CEM neurons and produces hermaphrodites which also lack other male-specific neurons found in the tail (White et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2007.

claim: ceh-30(n4289) males lack the male-specific CEM neurons in the head.
source: While ceh-30(n4289) males lack the male-specific CEM neurons in the head (Schwartz and Horvitz, 2007), mab-3(e1240) mutants display marked defects in male-tail formation including ray differentiation as well as in male specific circuitry in the head of the animal (Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwartz and Horvitz, 2007.

claim: mab-3(e1240) mutants display marked defects in male-tail formation including ray differentiation as well as in male specific circuitry in the head of the animal.
source: While ceh-30(n4289) males lack the male-specific CEM neurons in the head (Schwartz and Horvitz, 2007), mab-3(e1240) mutants display marked defects in male-tail formation including ray differentiation as well as in male specific circuitry in the head of the animal (Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yi et al., 2000.

claim: PKD-2 and LOV-1 constitute a TRP channel necessary for the function of the B-type ray neurons.
source: Similarly, PKD-2 and LOV-1 constitute a TRP channel necessary for the function of the B-type ray neurons—another set of male-specific neurons in the tail of the animal (Barr et al., 2001; Barr and Sternberg, 1999; Barrios et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barr et al., 2001; Barr and Sternberg, 1999; Barrios et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic 'feminization' of XO male animals can be achieved via the overexpression of the intracellular domain of the TRA-2 protein, which negatively interacts with FEM-3 to prevent TRA-1 degradation.
source: Complementary to masculinization, genetic 'feminization' of XO male animals can be achieved via the overexpression of the intracellular domain of the TRA-2 protein, which negatively interacts with FEM-3 to prevent TRA-1 degradation (Mehra et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mehra et al., 1999.
